title: Detection Strategy for Invisible Unicode
summary: This detection strategy looks for invisible Unicode characters inserted into text, file names and code where they serve no legitimate purpose. It covers technique T1027.018 and matters because zero width and bidirectional control characters can hide content, reverse how a string is displayed, or smuggle instructions into text that a human reviewer reads as harmless. The telemetry that makes it possible is mail message bodies and subjects, file and directory names from endpoint file system events, source code and document content from repositories, and editor or collaboration platform content records, all of which must be examined at code point level rather than as rendered text. In practice the strategy fails because invisible characters also arrive legitimately, for example zero width joiners in emoji sequences and bidirectional markers in bilingual documents, and because many log pipelines normalise or strip these characters before storage. Analysts therefore count and classify the characters, check the surrounding language, and alert on combinations that cannot be explained by normal text.

beginner.definition: Unicode is a standard that gives every character a number. Some characters have no width at all, so they are invisible on screen. This detection finds those hidden characters in text, file names and code.
beginner.whyItMatters: What you see is not always what the computer receives. An invisible character can change how a line of code is read. It can also carry hidden instructions in a message or a file name. A reviewer reading the screen sees nothing unusual, so the trick survives a quick check. Finding hidden characters lets you confirm the file or message is not what it appears to be.
howItWorks: You collect the raw text, such as an email body, a file name or a source file.
You look at each character by its code number, not by how it looks on screen.
You count characters that take no space, such as zero width spaces and joiners.
You flag direction control characters. These can make text display in reverse order.
You check the language of the text. A few joiners in emoji are normal, a block of them is not.
You alert with the file or message name and the exact code points for the analyst.
beginner.example: Think of a sign-in sheet where someone writes with invisible ink in the margin. The page looks clean to the receptionist, and the visible names are all correct. But a message is there for anyone who knows to look with the right lamp. Invisible Unicode characters are that ink. Your detection tool is the lamp.
takeaways: Always check text by code point, because rendered text can hide real content.
Normal text rarely contains many invisible characters, so volume is a strong clue.
Invisible characters in code or file names are far more suspicious than in prose.

objectives: Describe how zero width and bidirectional control characters can hide or reverse content in text
Inspect text at code point level using an escape aware view instead of rendered output
Set thresholds for the count of invisible characters that suit prose, file names and source code
Recognise legitimate uses such as zero width joiners in emoji and directional marks in bilingual text
Correlate hidden character findings with the file, message or commit that introduced them
Explain why log pipelines that normalise text can remove the very evidence you need
dataSources: Raw email message bodies and subject lines stored as unicode escape sequences rather than rendered text
Sysmon event 11 file creation records containing the full file name including non printable characters where the agent preserves them
Source code repository commit records and diff content stored with character level fidelity
Command line text from Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled, captured in escaped form
Collaboration platform content audit records for messages and document titles including raw character sequences
logic: The pattern is the presence of invisible or direction changing Unicode characters where plain text is expected. You inspect raw text fields from mail bodies, file names, source diffs and command lines, count the characters in the zero width and directional control ranges, and compare that count with the surrounding language and the file type. The malicious case is a cluster of zero width characters inside a source file, a script name, a document title or a command line, often mixed with characters from different scripts to create visually identical identifiers. The benign case is a small number of joiners inside emoji sequences, or directional marks in a document that genuinely mixes right to left and left to right text. Character class, count and location decide the alert, because a single joiner in a chat message and forty joiners in a script name are not the same event.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Invisible Unicode Characters in File Name or Command Line
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: file_event
# detection:
#   selection:
#     file_name|contains:
#       - '\u200b'
#       - '\u200c'
#       - '\u200d'
#       - '\u2060'
#       - '\u202e'
#       - '\ufeff'
#   filter_emoji:
#     file_name|re: '^[\\p{Emoji}]+$'
#   condition: selection and not filter_emoji
# level: medium
falsePositives: Emoji and emoji sequences in chat messages or file names that legitimately contain zero width joiners
Bilingual documents that use directional marks to display Arabic or Hebrew text correctly beside English
Byte order marks added automatically at the start of text files by some editors and export tools
Copy and paste from web pages that carries hidden formatting characters into an email or document
Localisation and machine translation pipelines that emit control characters while processing mixed script text
tuningNotes: Separate the rule into two severities: one for invisible characters in executable content, scripts, file names and command lines, and a much lower one for prose such as chat and document bodies. Allowlist the specific code point sequences your collaboration platform emits for emoji, then set a count threshold above the natural level of the remaining text so that a stray pasted character does not alert. Scope the first version to file names and command lines, where hidden characters have the clearest impact. Confirming that your log pipeline preserves these characters is essential, because a pipeline that strips them gives a false sense of coverage rather than a detection.
